Usually, this set consists of n distinct points, i.e., solutions of the degree n equation P (x) = y0 (see Fig. 2.1). But for some speciﬁc values of y this equation may have multiple roots. A multiple root of the equation P (x) = y is also a root of the equation P  (x) = 0. Deﬁnition 2.2.2 (Critical points and critical values). A point x ∈ C at which P  (x) = 0 is called a critical point of the polynomial P . The value y = P (x) of the polynomial at its critical point x is called a critical value. We say that a critical point x has multiplicity, or order, or degree k ≥ 2 if at this point P  (x) = 0, P  (x) = 0, . . . , P (k−1) (x) = 0, P (k) (x) 
= 0. Recall that we usually assign to each critical value y a partition of n whose parts are the multiplicities of the roots of the equation P (x) = y, and that the sequence of these partitions is called a passport. Since the derivative P  is a polynomial of degree n − 1, the polynomial P “usually” (that is, in the generic case) has n − 1 critical points of order 2 and n − 1 distinct critical values. But in some degenerate cases one may observe critical points of higher order, and/or the values of the polynomial at diﬀerent critical points may coincide. What we are interested in is the most degenerate case, when the set of critical values of P is as small as possible. Example 2.2.3. The polynomial P (x) = xn has only one critical point of order n (namely, x = 0), and only one critical value y = 0.

# Graphs on Surfaces and Their Applications

Sergei K. Lando, Alexander K. ZvonkinSpringer Science & Business Media, Dec 1, 2003 - Mathematics - 455 pages Graphs drawn on two-dimensional surfaces have always attracted researchers by their beauty and by the variety of difficult questions to which they give rise. The theory of such embedded graphs, which long seemed rather isolated, has witnessed the appearance of entirely unexpected new applications in recent decades, ranging from Galois theory to quantum gravity models, and has become a kind of a focus of a vast field of research. The book provides an accessible introduction to this new domain, including such topics as coverings of Riemann surfaces, the Galois group action on embedded graphs (Grothendieck's theory of "dessins d'enfants"), the matrix integral method, moduli spaces of curves, the topology of meromorphic functions, and combinatorial aspects of Vassiliev's knot invariants and, in an appendix by Don Zagier, the use of finite group representation theory. The presentation is concrete throughout, with numerous figures, examples (including computer calculations) and exercises, and should appeal to both graduate students and researchers. [Input]

L3@P0: Abstract. We give an account of the theory of dessins d’enfants which is both
L4@P0: elementary and self-contained. We describe the equivalence of many categories
L5@P0: (graphs embedded nicely on surfaces, finite sets with certain permutations,
L6@P0: certain field extensions, and some classes of algebraic curves), some of which are
L7@P0: naturally endowed with an action of the absolute Galois group of the rational
L8@P0: field. We prove that the action is faithful. Eventually we prove that Gal(Q/Q)
L9@P0: embeds into the Grothendieck-Teichmüller group GTc 0 introduced by Drinfeld.
L10@P0: There are explicit approximations of GTc 0 by finite groups, and we hope to
L11@P0: encourage computations in this area.
L12@P0: Our treatment includes a result which has not appeared in the literature
L13@P0: yet: the action of Gal(Q/Q) on the subset of regular dessins – that is, those

L46@P0-1: ⋆Introduction
L47@P1: The story of dessins d’enfants (children’s drawings) is best told in two episodes.
L48@P1: The first side of the story is a surprising unification of different-looking theories:
L49@P1: graphs embedded nicely on surfaces, finite sets with certain permutations, certain
L50@P1: field extensions, and some classes of algebraic curves (some over C, some over Q), all
L51@P1: turn out to define equivalent categories. This result follows from powerful and yet
L52@P1: very classical theorems, mostly from the 19th century, such as the correspondence
L53@P1: between Riemann surfaces and their fields of meromorphic functions (of course
L54@P1: known to Riemann himself), or the basic properties of the fundamental group (dating back to Poincaré).
L55@P1: One of our goals with the present paper is to give an account of this theory that
L56@P1: sticks to elementary methods, as we believe it should. (For example we shall never
L57@P1: need to appeal to “Weil’s rigidity criterion”, as is most often done in the literature on
L58@P1: the subject; note that it is also possible, in fact, to read most of this paper without
L59@P1: any knowledge of algebraic curves.) Our development is moreover as self-contained
L60@P1: as is reasonable: that is, while this paper is not the place to develop the theory
L61@P1: of Riemann surfaces, Galois extensions or covering spaces from scratch – we shall
L62@P1: refer to basic textbooks for these – we give complete arguments from there. Also,
L63@P1: we have striven to state the results in terms of actual equivalences of categories, a
L64@P1: slick language which unfortunately is not always employed in the usual sources.
L65@P1: The term dessins d’enfants was coined by Grothendieck in [Gro97], in which a
L66@P1: vast programme was laid out, giving the theory a new thrust which is the second side
L67@P1: of the story we wish to tell. In a nutshell, some of the categories mentioned above
L68@P1: naturally carry an action of Gal(Q/Q), the absolute Galois group of the rational
L69@P1: field. This group therefore acts on the set of isomorphism classes of objects in any
L70@P1: of the equivalent categories; in particular one can define an action of the absolute
L71@P1: Galois group on graphs embedded on surfaces. In this situation however, the nature
L72@P1: of the Galois action is really very mysterious - it is hoped that, by studying it, light
L73@P1: may be shed on the structure of Gal(Q/Q). It is the opportunity to bring some
L74@P1: kind of basic, visual geometry to bear in the study of the absolute Galois group
L75@P1: that makes dessins d’enfants – embedded graphs – so attractive.
L76@P1: In this paper we explain carefully, again relying only on elementary methods, how
L77@P1: one defines the action, and how one proves that it is faithful. This last property
L78@P1: is clearly crucial if we are to have any hope of studying Gal(Q/Q) by considering
L79@P1: graphs. We devote some space to the search for invariants of dessins belonging to
L80@P1: the same Galois orbit, a major objective in the field.
L81@P1: When a group acts faithfully on something, we can usually obtain an embedding
L82@P1: of it in some automorphism group. In our case, this leads to the GrothendieckTeichmüller group GTd, first introduced by Drinfeld in [Dri90], and proved to contain Gal(Q/Q) by Ihara in [Iha94]. While trying to describe Ihara’s proof in any
L83@P1: detail would carry us beyond the scope of this paper, we present a complete, elementary argument establishing that Gal(Q/Q) embeds into the slightly larger
L84@P1: group GTd0 also defined by Drinfeld. In fact we work with a group GT isomorphic
L85@P1: to GTd0, and which is an inverse limit
L86@P1: GT = limnGT (n) ;
L87@P1: here GT (n) is a certain subgroup of Out(Hn) for an explicitly defined finite
L88@P1: group Hn. So describing Hn and GT (n) for some n large enough gives rough
L89@P1: information about Gal(Q/Q) – and it is possible to do so in finite time.
L90@P1: In turn, we shall see that understanding Hn amounts, in a sense, to understanding all finite groups generated by two elements, whose order is less than n. We land
L91@P1: back on our feet: from the first part of this paper, those groups are in one to one
L92@P1: correspondence with some embedded graphs, called regular, exhibiting maximal
L93@P1: symmetry. The classification of “regular maps”, as they are sometimes called, is a
L94@P1: classical topic which is still alive today.

L101@P3: field F ⊆ Q, being a group of all automorphisms of Q fixing F, is necessarily
